prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, in which neutral atoms trapped at a magic wavelength brought the accuracy and stability of optical frequency standards to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: After the full first-round exchange I keep the optical lattice clock as a single prize part, and I do not change my configuration. What moved in round 1 was the committee, not me: Johansson, Mehlig and Pearce arrived at B027 from other opening first choices, and they did so for scientific reasons I find independent of mine, namely a bounded invention, reproduction in several laboratories, and a two-name credit with no evident missing principal. Scientifically, Katori's magic-wavelength condition is a new idea, not a refinement of the comb or the ion trap. It removes the differential light shift for many neutral atoms at once, so that the clock transition can be probed free of Doppler and recoil effects with the statistical power of a large ensemble. Ye's group demonstrated what the idea can do, with systematic uncertainty and stability near 10^-18, many-body operation, and centimetre-scale tests of gravitational time dilation. I treat the count of supporters as irrelevant to the argument. The reason to rank B027 first is that it is the only shortlisted configuration where the discovery, its maturity and its exact credit all hold at the same time. The citation should name the optical lattice clock itself, not precision spectroscopy or optical clocks in general, so that it cannot be read as a repeat of 2005 or 2012.
statement.case_against: The strongest argument against remains overlap with the lineage honoured in 1997/2001, 2005 and 2012. I hold that the magic-wavelength lattice is a separate concept, but the clock does rest on comb and ultrastable-laser technology that earlier laureates and others built, and the committee should say so openly instead of treating the matter as closed. Second, the redefinition of the second has not happened, so the largest practical consequence is still prospective, and the reach into dark matter and varying constants is more promise than result. Third, ion-clock pioneers, the early Sr and Yb lattice groups and ultrastable-laser developers fall outside the two names; Olsson's point that part of Ye's contribution is the pushing of accuracy and not a distinct concept is fair, and I accept that a narrow citation purchases clean attribution at the price of leaving real contributors uncredited. Finally, a measurement-science prize competes poorly with a new observational window or a new phase of matter if one weighs headline appeal, and I do not claim otherwise.

responses.point: Eriksson moved to B057 (Kane, Mele, Molenkamp) as his preferred prize, citing breadth of ranking, fifteen years of independent confirmation and a natural theory-plus-experiment trio, and he thinks B027 needs justification if it is not honoured.
responses.response: I take the confirmation record and the theory-plus-experiment structure seriously, and I still rank B057 second. I disagree that breadth of ranking should settle it, because seven members placing it somewhere on their ballots mostly reflects that it is a safe second choice, and the chair's summary shows that six of eight members, including those who placed it second, would not put it first. The deciding issue is the credit. A citation framed around the Z2 classification and the HgTe observation leaves out Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, whose proposal identified HgTe as the platform, and the three-dimensional work of Fu, Moore, Balents, Hasan and Cava. A three-person cap forces that choice, and I cannot make it from the supplied record. On 2016 I accept his distinction between phase transitions and the Z2 insulator, so I do not regard the overlap as disqualifying. If the committee could agree a credit that withstands the omission of the HgTe proposers, I would revisit it, but that is a prospective condition and not the position today.

responses.point: Olsson prefers B053 (Rose, Urban, Haider) as an enabling invention with traceable authorship, says she would not insist if the clock or topological candidates are judged stronger, and thinks Ye's role may be partly accuracy and not a distinct concept.
responses.response: I appreciate that she states the weakness of her own candidate openly, and I agree that authorship of the corrector is easy to document. My difficulty is the same one she names: it is instrumentation, and Krivanek's parallel STEM work makes the three-name credit contestable under the cap. On her point about Ye, I think the division is defensible. Katori supplied the magic-wavelength concept and the first lattice demonstration, and Ye's group showed that the concept scales to 10^-18 with many-body operation and the time-dilation measurement. Whether pushing accuracy is a prize-worthy step in its own right is a judgment call, but it is the step that turned the idea into a result that others could reproduce, and I think that justifies the credit. Her stated willingness to yield also suggests we are not far apart in practice.

responses.point: Pearce, the Chair, moved from IceCube (B041) to B027 for breadth of support and credit cleanliness, and kept B041 as first alternative, while accepting that a new observational window is less incremental than the clock.
responses.response: I agree with him that attribution, not scientific superiority, is what decides the order, and I think the committee should be honest that this is the argument. On IceCube I keep B041 as an alternative, not a preferred part. Halzen and Karle alone do not capture a collaboration of this size and an AMANDA predecessor, and Gaisser, Becker and Kowalski could be argued, so the credit is not yet defensible within three names. His chair question about whether non-astroparticle members should defer on the decisive pair is a fair one; I cannot judge the internal history of the experiment, and I would defer to his and Johansson's reading of that history, but a deference that leaves the credit unresolved does not make B041 ready for a vote this year.

responses.point: Mehlig moved from flocking (B002) to B027 on attribution cleanliness, asks whether the unfinished redefinition of the second argues for waiting or for acting, and says the many-body Fermi-gas operation is itself a statistical-physics result.
responses.response: I agree that the many-body, spin-polarised operation matters, and it is part of why I regard the achievement as physics and not only engineering. On his question about the second, I think the redefinition is the wrong clock to set by. The physics result, independent reproduction at 10^-18 in several laboratories, is already established, and the prize citation should rest on that and not on a metrological decision taken by another body. Waiting for the redefinition would make the prize depend on a committee outside ours; acting now does not anticipate it, provided the citation does not mention the second. I note that his own B002 remains the deepest conceptual case on the list in his view, but I agree with him that its quantitative confirmation and the Vicsek versus Toner-Tu attribution are not ready.

responses.point: Lindroth argues that the comb gave a way to count optical cycles whereas the lattice clock holds many atoms unperturbed, so the 2005 precedent is answered by the citation, and that the pending redefinition does not weaken the case.
responses.response: I agree and I think her formulation is the sharpest answer to the overlap objection: the comb is a counter, the lattice clock is a protected oscillator, and 2005 did not address the latter. Her expertise in polarisabilities and blackbody shifts is the right check on the 10^-18 claim, and I would ask that the committee record that the uncertainty budgets rest on independent evaluation by JILA, RIKEN, PTB, NIST and SYRTE and not on a single laboratory. Where I stay a little more cautious than she does is that the separation holds for the concept but not completely for the toolkit, since the comb and the ultrastable laser are indispensable parts of the 10^-18 result; the citation wording is how we acknowledge that.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts the magic-wavelength lattice as a new concept distinct from the 2005 frequency-comb and 2012 single-ion prizes, which I judge to hold but not beyond challenge.
Whether ion-clock pioneers, early Sr and Yb lattice groups or ultrastable-laser developers have a claim that a two-name prize cannot represent, and whether leaving them out is acceptable.

Whether a credit for B057 could be drawn that survives the omission of Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang and the three-dimensional contributors; I currently think not, and this is the margin on which my ranking depends.
Whether IceCube (B041) can obtain a defensible credit, since I cannot independently assess the internal history of AMANDA and IceCube.
Whether a two-part configuration is feasible within three names; with B027 using two, I have found no second part that can be added with one name.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile and I am not aware of a change since round 1. My documented connections are my PhD supervisor David Gross, my early mentor Hector Rubinstein, my co-author Thomas Van Riet and the Uppsala theory group, and none is connected to any shortlisted candidate or credited name. I note the proximity disclosures of Olsson, Johansson, Lindroth, Kroll, Eriksson and Pearce, and I think they should be weighed as stated, since none reports a documented personal tie to a credited person for B027 and the committee has no need to apply a recusal to the preferred configuration.
